questions.questionText: What is "vectorization" in numpy, and why does it matter?
options: Performing element-wise operations on entire arrays via optimized compiled code instead of explicit Python loops, which is dramatically faster
A way to visualize data as charts
It has no performance benefit over plain Python loops
questions.correctAnswer: Performing element-wise operations on entire arrays via optimized compiled code instead of explicit Python loops, which is dramatically faster
questions.explanation: Vectorized numpy operations avoid slow Python-level loops, running instead as optimized compiled code — typically 10-100x faster for array operations of any real size.

questions.questionText: What does "broadcasting" let you do in numpy?
options: Combine arrays of different shapes in an operation (e.g. a scalar or smaller array applied across a larger one) without manually resizing them
Convert numpy arrays into Python lists
Broadcasting is not a real numpy feature
questions.correctAnswer: Combine arrays of different shapes in an operation (e.g. a scalar or smaller array applied across a larger one) without manually resizing them
questions.explanation: Broadcasting follows specific shape-compatibility rules to let numpy implicitly apply an operation across arrays of different shapes, exactly what makes W @ x + b work cleanly.

questions.questionText: What does boolean indexing like a[a > 2] do?
options: It converts the array to boolean (True/False) values
It selects only the elements of the array that satisfy the given condition
It sorts the array in ascending order
It raises an error since numpy doesn't support conditional selection
questions.correctAnswer: It selects only the elements of the array that satisfy the given condition
questions.explanation: a > 2 produces a boolean mask, and indexing the array with that mask returns only the elements where the condition is true — a common, concise numpy pattern.
